THE SAVOY MALE AND FEMALE COLLEGE  79

STUDENT ORGANIZATIONS

TEMPERANCE SOCIETIES.—Some of the student organizations at Savoy College reported in Y.M.C.A. Convention Reports show that the College was actively participating in the high moral tone, in keeping with the high moral tone, social and religious improvement.

The Band of Hope was organized in the early years of the school by the students under the leadership of the Reverend Dick Gay. The children accepted it eagerly and printed themselves a constitution and by-laws and called themselves, with "Savoy College" and printed on it in black lettering, a card to be carried in the coat pocket by those who joined, and those who joined were given to the occasion, to "Touch not, taste not, handle not," using one of the songs of the college drinking song, Krambemball, which can roughly be translated.

MY DRINK SHALL BE THE FLOWING FOUNTAIN

The students sang it with open-minded occasion. The song was suggested and received; Misses Pamela Paxton and Frankie Chenoweth were "right and left-hand supporters" of the Band of Hope movement, and were thus honored with the "up-in-front" chairs that were served at each of the meetings.⁶⁵

It is Lizzie Paxton who carries in the writing an account of the following episode which as well reflects "negativism," as a chore. "I recall that many of the young temperance ladies would sign the pledge to bring some of the young men around.

Mrs. Wyatt, wife of a Savoy physician, was the first organizer of the Women's Christian Temperance Union to operate for young ladies of the College and for town women. Miss Pamela Paxton taught during the year 1886-1887 at the College, and Miss Frankie Chenoweth taught in the fall of that year.

Biographies of many prominent men in the much-quoted Biographical Souvenir of 1889 show their membership in the Order of Good Templars; and in the Temperance Literary Societies, Professor Pritchett having returned to the work of Modern Languages, was added to the faculty. It is stated that in 1888-1887, and Miss Lottie Daniels, about two women of distinction. The first leaders of the Savoy temperance movement, by the Order of Good Templars, were Mrs. Jed Williams, from the studio near the campus, were Miss Jennie Lacy, of Bonham, who taught the last year of the school's existence.
